Loans you already owe and your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months can lower that amount. The calculator subtracts what you owe. It returns the largest new loan allowed and the payment for the amount you want to borrow. Start with Vested account balance, then enter any Plan loans you owe now and your Highest plan-loan balance, last 12 months. Add the Loan amount you want, Interest rate (APR), Term (years), Payments per year and Loan purpose to see the repayment figures and any rule warnings. In our internal modeling, we applied the loan-limit formula to a $60,000 vested balance with no earlier loans. The limit on all plan loans together was $30,000, leaving $30,000 available for a new loan. For a $10,000 loan at an example 8% annual percentage rate (APR), the payment was $202.76 per month over 5 years. Total interest was $2,165.84, and total repaid was $12,165.84. Those payment figures use a level-payment schedule. They do not establish the rate your plan would charge. Change the inputs below to see how a different loan amount, rate or payment schedule changes the result. $30,000 largest new loan at $60,000 vested $202.76 payment on $10,000 over 5 years $2,166 total interest Share Interactive — edit any field How the Loan Limit Is Calculated Under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(2)(A) , the limit on all plan loans together is the smaller of two amounts. The first starts at $50,000 and falls by the amount your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded what you owe today. The second is the greater of half your vested balance or $10,000. The calculator compares those two amounts, then subtracts Plan loans you owe now to show room for a new loan. That distinction matters when you have borrowed before: the limit on all loans is not the same as the amount you can take out today. Enter the highest balance even if you have since paid down that loan, because the earlier balance can reduce the $50,000 prong. Vested balance Owed now 12-month peak Limit on all loans Room for a new loan $15,000 None None $10,000 $10,000 $60,000 None None $30,000 $30,000 $100,000 None None $50,000 $50,000 $200,000 None None $50,000 $50,000 $200,000 $10,000 $20,000 $40,000 $30,000 $200,000 $20,000 $50,000 $20,000 $0 The $15,000 balance produces a $10,000 limit because half the vested balance is $7,500 and the statutory floor is higher. At a $100,000 vested balance with nothing owed, half the balance reaches the $50,000 cap. A higher vested balance does not raise that cap: the $200,000 example with no loans also has a $50,000 limit. The prior-loan example shows why the two subtractions must stay separate. With $10,000 owed and a $20,000 peak, the peak exceeds today's balance by $10,000, reducing the $50,000 prong to $40,000. The calculator then subtracts the $10,000 still owed from the $40,000 limit, leaving $30,000 for a new loan. Subtracting the $10,000 a second time would count it twice and wrongly leave $20,000 of room. In the last table row, the peak reduces that prong to $20,000, which equals the amount already owed. The result is no room for another loan under the federal cap, even though the vested balance is higher. Repayment Rules the Calculator Checks A general-purpose plan loan must be repayable within 5 years under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(2)(B) and (C) . The statute makes an exception for a loan used to buy a dwelling that will become the participant's main home within a reasonable time. It also requires substantially level payments at least quarterly. Choose General purpose or Buy a main home under Loan purpose so the calculator can check the term you entered. It warns when a general-purpose term exceeds 5 years or when Payments per year is less often than quarterly. A green note means the entered amount, term and payment frequency fit the federal rules the calculator checks. It does not mean your plan offers loans. The calculator also warns when Loan amount you want exceeds Largest new loan allowed. Under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(1) , the portion outside the qualifying loan rules is treated as a distribution. Use the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator for a tax estimate rather than treating that excess as an ordinary loan payment. For payments, the calculator divides APR by Payments per year to get the periodic rate. It multiplies Term (years) by Payments per year to get the number of payments, then applies payment = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n). Each payment covers that period's interest. The remainder reduces the loan balance. Example rate Monthly payment on $10,000 Term Total interest 6% $193.33 5 years $1,599.68 8% $202.76 5 years $2,165.84 10% $212.47 5 years $2,748.23 These rates are examples to replace with the rate in your plan terms. Payment frequency changes the schedule too: at an example 8%, the same $10,000 loan over 5 years has 20 quarterly payments of $611.57 each. At that rate, paying every two weeks produces 130 payments of $93.45 each. A longer permitted main-home term can lower each payment while increasing total interest in the supplied example. A $30,000 loan at an example 8% costs $608.29 per month over 5 years, with $6,497.51 in total interest. Over 15 years, the main-home example costs $286.70 per month, with $21,605.21 in total interest. Run your own amount and rate before relying on any example payment. The federal limit and repayment rules determine whether the amount qualifies as a loan rather than a distribution, while the plan document decides whether borrowing is available at all. If the plan document has no loan provision, this calculator cannot make a loan available. Borrowing From a Solo 401(k) The same federal loan-limit formula applies to an owner-only 401(k), so a solo 401k loan calculator needs no separate limit setting. The plan document must provide for loans, and a provision alone does not establish that a participant loan avoids a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. 4975(d)(1) . An owner is generally a key employee under 26 U.S.C. 416(i) , so interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible under 72(p)(3). Read the solo section of the 401(k) loan rules guide , then enter your vested balance in the calculator above. What the Calculator Does Not Include The calculator does not include plan fees or determine your plan's interest rate or loan limits. Enter the interest rate and loan amount you want in the calculator. The calculator does not estimate income tax or additional tax if a loan is treated as a distribution. Use the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator for a tax estimate, and ask a tax professional about a missed payment. The calculator assigns no market return to money while it is out of the plan and does not determine where repayments are credited. Account for the borrowed money's time out of the market separately. Whether interest you repay is credited to your account depends on the plan document. The calculator does not compare a plan loan with another borrowing source. Use 401(k) loan vs HELOC to compare the borrowing choices. Frequently asked questions How are 401k loan amounts calculated? The federal limit on all your plan loans is the smaller of a reduced $50,000 cap or the greater of half your vested balance and $10,000. The cap falls by any amount your highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded what you owe today. Subtract loans you owe now from the resulting limit to find room for a new loan. With $60,000 vested and no earlier loans, the limit and room for a new loan are both $30,000. How much would a $10,000 401(k) loan cost per month over 5 years? A $10,000 loan paid monthly over 5 years costs $202.76 per month at an example 8% APR. At example rates of 6% and 10%, the payments are $193.33 and $212.47 per month, respectively. These are example rates. A plan sets its own rate. Enter the interest rate from your plan terms in this calculator to see your own payment. How many 401(k) loans can you have at once? The federal loan-limit text states no maximum number of simultaneous plan loans. It counts every outstanding plan loan toward the limit. Your plan document decides whether loans are available and whether it limits their number. Enter all Plan loans you owe now to calculate the room left for another loan. Can I take a loan from a solo 401(k)? A solo 401(k) can provide for participant loans, but its plan document must allow them. The same federal loan-limit formula applies to an owner-only plan, and a plan provision alone does not settle the prohibited-transaction requirements. Read the solo section of the 401(k) loan rules guide before using the calculator for a proposed loan. What happens if I do not repay a 401(k) loan? A plan loan that fails to meet the qualifying loan rules can be treated as a distribution under 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(1). The calculator does not determine the tax consequences of a missed payment. Ask a tax professional to confirm those consequences, and use the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator for a tax estimate. Your plan document determines whether loans are offered, the interest rate, fees and any limit on the number of loans. The hard money loan calculator shows that cost alongside your loan amount, cash to close, monthly interest-only payment, and balloon payoff. It also returns loan-to-cost and loan-to-after-repair-value percentages. Enter an after-repair value to see profit before tax. Start with the purchase price, rehab budget, and terms from your lender quote. A hard money loan here means a short-term loan with points and fees at closing, interest-only payments, and repayment of the full balance at exit. The figures already in the calculator are example inputs that carry no lender data. Replace them with the terms for the deal you want to calculate. In our internal modeling, we ran one example deal and found a $20,900 total financing cost on a $230,000 loan held for 6 months. The example uses a $200,000 purchase and a $50,000 rehab budget. The lender advances 90% of the purchase and 100% of the rehab, with a 12% annual percentage rate (APR). Closing charges are 2 points and $2,500 in other fees. The result includes $13,800 in interest and $7,100 in points and fees. Repayment of the $230,000 loan balance is a separate balloon payoff, so it does not appear as another financing charge. You can reproduce the example with the starting inputs, then enter your own terms to see how the cost changes. $20,900 total financing cost on the example terms $2,300 monthly interest-only payment 92% loan to cost Share Interactive — edit any field How the Cost Adds Up Total financing cost adds the points paid at closing, lender and other fees, interest during the months held, and any extension fee. Points equal the loan amount multiplied by the points percentage. For each month, interest equals the outstanding balance multiplied by the APR and divided by 12. Piece Example amount Loan $230,000 Points $4,600 Other fees $2,500 Interest-only payment $2,300 a month Interest over 6 months $13,800 Total financing cost $20,900 Balloon payoff $230,000 Cash to close $27,100 The loan combines $180,000 advanced against the purchase with $50,000 advanced for rehab. The $20,000 down payment, $4,600 in points, and $2,500 in other fees make cash to close $27,100. Cash to close describes money needed at closing. It is not the same measure as total financing cost. Interest-only payments cover interest while the balance remains outstanding. In this example, the $2,300 monthly payment does not pay down the $230,000 loan. The Balloon payoff at exit line therefore shows the full loan balance, separate from the interest and closing charges already counted in financing cost. Simple annualized cost divides total financing cost by the loan amount and then by the years held. It is 18.17% for this example, which includes points and fees as well as interest. It is not an internal rate of return (IRR): the calculation does not use the dates of individual cash flows to produce an IRR. Loan to Cost and Loan to ARV Explained Loan to cost (LTC) divides the loan amount by the purchase price plus the rehab budget. For the example, the $230,000 loan divided by the $200,000 purchase and $50,000 rehab budget gives 92%. This percentage describes the share of those project costs covered by the modeled loan. It does not include financing charges or other holding costs in the denominator. Loan to after-repair value (ARV) divides the loan amount by the after-repair value you enter. At an example ARV of $330,000, the $230,000 loan produces a loan-to-ARV figure of 69.7%. Leave ARV blank if you only need the loan-cost calculation. The loan-to-ARV and profit figures need an ARV input. The profit calculation starts with ARV and subtracts selling costs, purchase price, rehab budget, total financing cost, and other holding costs. At $330,000 ARV and 6% selling costs, the modeled selling costs are $19,800. Other holding costs of $1,000 a month add up to $6,000 over 6 months. With those inputs, Profit before tax is $33,300. That figure counts the $20,900 financing cost as an expense, alongside the purchase and rehab costs. The balloon payoff is not subtracted again: the purchase and rehab amounts already represent the project spending financed in part by the loan. Cash to close and profit answer different questions. Cash to close shows the modeled amount needed to complete the purchase with the stated advance percentages, points, and fees. Profit before tax uses the entered sale value and costs to show the modeled outcome at exit. What Moves the Total Most Holding time changes the example's financing cost by $2,300 for each additional month at the full loan balance. The calculator's What moves the total table also changes points and APR while keeping the other example inputs fixed. These figures show how much each specified change moves the $20,900 starting total. Change Total financing cost Change from example Hold for 3 months $14,000 $6,900 lower Hold for 9 months $27,800 $6,900 higher Charge 1 point $18,600 $2,300 lower Charge 3 points $23,200 $2,300 higher Use 10% APR $18,600 $2,300 lower Use 14% APR $23,200 $2,300 higher A point equals 1% of the loan amount. On the $230,000 example loan, changing the charge by one point changes closing cost by $2,300. The interest-rate rows show the same dollar change for the stated APR changes over the example holding period. They do not tell you what a lender will quote. An extension can change both interest and fees. On the example loan, a 3-month extension with a 1% extension fee adds $6,900 of interest and a $2,300 fee. That is $9,200 more in financing cost, bringing the total to $30,100. The extension months accrue interest on the full loan balance. The rehab funding choice changes when interest begins on the rehab advance. If rehab money is Funded at closing, the full loan accrues interest from the first month. If it is Drawn evenly each month, the modeled rehab balance grows in equal monthly portions. The purchase advance remains outstanding throughout. For the example's 6-month hold, even draws reduce interest from $13,800 to $12,550. Total financing cost falls from $20,900 to $19,650. Select the funding method that matches the schedule you are modeling rather than treating the two totals as interchangeable quotes. Time held is the larger lever in the stated comparison: a 3-month change moves the total by $6,900. A one-point change moves it by $2,300. Different draw timing, extension terms, points, or fees would change the answer, so use the terms for the particular loan you are comparing. The hard money loan calculator cannot supply a lender quote. If you need a quoted rate or fee, obtain those terms from a lender before using its output to compare financing costs. Enter the terms from your lender quote in the calculator above and read the Total financing cost line. What the Calculator Does Not Include The calculator does not subtract income tax from profit. For the tax issue associated with a short-term flip, read flipping houses and its tax trap and keep the displayed profit labeled before tax. Draw inspection fees are not included automatically. If your terms list them, add their amount to Lender, document and other fees. Default interest and prepayment minimums are not modeled. Read the repayment terms in the quote before relying on the displayed interest total for a different payoff schedule. Profit before tax ignores any costs you have not entered, as well as tax. Enter the available selling and holding costs, and treat the result as a calculation based only on those inputs. The calculator does not compare this loan with a different short-term financing route. Use bridge loan vs HELOC to examine that choice, then enter separate terms in the bridge loan calculator . Frequently asked questions How do you calculate loan to cost? Divide the loan amount by the purchase price plus the rehab budget. The example combines a $200,000 purchase and a $50,000 rehab budget. A $230,000 loan against those costs gives a 92% loan-to-cost figure. This calculation uses the stated purchase and rehab costs and does not add interest or fees to that denominator. Are hard money loans interest only? This calculator models interest-only payments each month and repayment of the full balance at exit. Its monthly payment does not reduce the balloon payoff. Your lender's terms determine whether the loan you are considering follows that structure. Use the payment and payoff terms in your quote when interpreting the results. How much do points add to a hard money loan? Points add the loan amount multiplied by the points percentage to closing cost. On the $230,000 example loan, 2 points add $4,600. Each point changes that loan's closing cost by $2,300. Points are included in Total financing cost even though they are paid at closing rather than through monthly interest. What does an extension cost? An extension adds interest for the extra months and any extension fee entered. In the example, 3 extra months add $6,900 in interest. A 1% fee adds another $2,300, bringing the extension's added financing cost to $9,200. The calculator applies interest during extension months to the full loan balance. This bridge loan calculator returns that total cost and the monthly outlay for carrying both homes. It also returns the net proceeds left after the sale pays off the old mortgage, the bridge loan and selling costs. Start with the expected sale price and old mortgage payoff. Then enter the bridge loan terms and the number of months you expect to carry both homes. The figures already in the calculator are examples that carry no lender data. Replace them with terms from your own lender quote. In our internal modeling, we ran one example sale through the calculator and found a $7,000 bridge loan cost after 6 months. The example uses a $400,000 sale price, a $200,000 old mortgage payoff, and a $100,000 bridge loan. At 10% annual percentage rate (APR) with 2% origination, the loan accrues $5,000 in interest and $2,000 in fees. Selling costs of 6% leave $69,000 in net proceeds. Enter your own terms below to see how a different sale date changes the result. $7,000 bridge cost over 6 months on the example terms $69,000 net proceeds from the old home Share Interactive — edit any field What a Bridge Loan Costs Month by Month Bridge interest is simple interest: multiply the loan by its APR, divide by 12, then multiply by the months until the old home sells. Fees equal the loan multiplied by the origination percentage, plus other fees charged once. Bridge loan cost adds those fees to interest. The calculation assumes interest is repaid from the sale proceeds at payoff. The example below holds the sale price, loan terms, selling costs, and monthly home payments fixed. Only the time until sale changes. Each row shows the bridge cost alongside the separate outlay for carrying both homes. Months to sell Interest Bridge cost Overlap outlay Net proceeds 3 $2,500 $4,500 $12,900 $71,500 6 $5,000 $7,000 $25,800 $69,000 9 $7,500 $9,500 $38,700 $66,500 12 $10,000 $12,000 $51,600 $64,000 Monthly overlap outlay adds the new mortgage payment to the old home's monthly carrying costs. Enter the old mortgage payment, taxes, insurance, and utilities in that carrying-cost field. With a $2,500 new mortgage payment and $1,800 in old home carrying costs, the outlay is $4,300 each month. The overlap total tells you how much cash you need for those home payments while waiting for a sale. It is separate from the bridge loan cost shown in the table. Under the calculator's payoff assumption, bridge interest reduces sale proceeds rather than appearing in the monthly overlap outlay. Selling costs equal the sale price multiplied by the selling-cost percentage. Net proceeds then subtract the old mortgage payoff, bridge loan, bridge cost, and selling costs from the sale price. In the example, $24,000 of selling costs leaves $69,000 after those deductions. The origination fee is charged once in this calculation, even if the sale takes longer than expected. If the old home sells after 0 months, the example bridge cost is the $2,000 fee alone. With no origination fee, the 6-month bridge cost falls to $5,000 and net proceeds rise to $71,000. Enter any other one-time fees separately so they appear in the bridge cost. How Much You Can Borrow The calculator estimates a borrowing ceiling only when you enter your lender's maximum combined loan-to-value limit. It multiplies the expected sale price by that limit and subtracts the old mortgage payoff. That gives you a figure to compare with your planned bridge loan. For the example sale, an entered limit of 80% produces a maximum of $120,000. The calculation applies 80% to the $400,000 expected sale price, then subtracts the $200,000 old mortgage payoff. The entered limit is an example. It is no standard lender limit and no loan offer. Your lender's quote supplies the limit, rate, fees, and term. If you do not have a combined loan-to-value figure, leave that optional field empty rather than treating the example as an available borrowing amount. You can still estimate bridge cost and net proceeds using the loan amount and terms you enter. A higher bridge loan amount affects more than the amount repaid at sale. Because interest is calculated from the loan amount, changing the bridge amount also changes interest and the net proceeds calculation. Origination fees change with the loan amount when you enter an origination percentage. Use the amount you intend to borrow when comparing the calculator's cost with the cash you expect from the old home. The maximum-borrowing output and the net-proceeds output answer different questions. The first applies an entered lender limit to the expected sale price and old payoff. The second subtracts the bridge repayment, its cost, and selling costs from that sale price. Read both before deciding whether the entered bridge amount fits your sale plan. When the Old Home Sells Late A later sale raises bridge interest and extends the monthly outlay for carrying both homes. In the example, each extra month adds $833.33 of bridge interest and lowers net proceeds by $833.33. The home payments continue separately at $4,300 a month under the example inputs. Use the calculator's "If the old home sells in" table to compare sale dates. It shows the entered timeline alongside 3, 6, and 9 months, so you can see the cost of a delay without changing the inputs repeatedly. The Copy results button lets you keep the figures from the scenario you entered. The optional Alternative cost, per month field compares the bridge's fees and interest with a monthly cost you enter. Break-even months equal bridge fees divided by the alternative's monthly cost minus bridge monthly interest. The calculation produces a break-even point only when the alternative costs more per month than bridge interest. Against an example alternative costing $1,500 a month with no up-front fee, the bridge costs less once the old home takes more than 3.0 months to sell. If the home sells sooner, the bridge costs more than that alternative. If the alternative costs no more than the bridge's $833.33 monthly interest, the bridge never costs less under this comparison. A sale may also leave too little to repay everything. If the old mortgage payoff rises from $200,000 to $300,000, the example produces negative $31,000 in net proceeds. The calculator warns when the sale does not cover the old mortgage, bridge loan, bridge cost, and selling costs. That result means you would bring cash to closing. For another way to compare financing the overlap, see bridge loan vs HELOC . For a related guide, see the guide to buying and selling a house at the same time . Use the calculator's cost figures for the bridge loan itself, rather than assuming the sale date or lender terms will match the examples. Bridge cost rises with the months until sale, so price a timeline that fits your plan before committing. This calculator cannot supply a lender quote for someone who needs an offered rate, fee, term, or borrowing limit. A longer sale, different fees, or interest paid monthly instead of at payoff would change the answer. Enter your own months to sell and lender quote in the bridge loan calculator above, then read the Bridge loan cost line. What the Calculator Does Not Include The calculator leaves out closing costs on the new home. Budget for those separately when working out the cash needed for the purchase. The calculator leaves out taxes on the sale. Keep any sale-related tax amount separate from the net proceeds shown here. The calculator does not model prepayment terms or lender-specific rules. Use the terms in your lender quote when deciding how the calculated cost applies to a loan offer. The calculator does not price an investment purchase financed with a different short-term loan. Use the hard money loan calculator for that loan instead. Frequently asked questions Does a bridge loan cost more? It depends on the cost you compare it with. Enter an alternative monthly cost in the calculator to compare it with the bridge's fees and interest. Against the example alternative costing $1,500 a month, the break-even point is 3.0 months. For a comparison of financing choices, see bridge loan vs HELOC . How much bridge loan can I get? The amount depends on the combined loan-to-value limit in your lender's quote. The calculator uses an entered limit and expected sale price, then subtracts the old mortgage payoff to estimate the most you could borrow under that limit. An example 80% limit gives $120,000 for the example sale. No limit on this page is a standard lender limit or a loan offer. How long does a bridge loan last? The term comes from your lender's quote. This calculator assumes no standard term. Enter the months until the old home sells to calculate interest through that sale date. The calculator also shows how the cost and net proceeds change at other sale dates. If interest is paid monthly rather than at payoff, the displayed monthly outlay does not include those interest payments. A loan from a qualified employer plan is treated as a distribution under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(1)(A) unless it stays within the amount limit, is repaid within 5 years (longer if it buys your main home), and is repaid in substantially level payments at least quarterly. To see how a permanent withdrawal works, read How to Withdraw From a 401(k) or try the 401(k) early withdrawal calculator . Tools for this journey 401(k) loan calculator → 401(k) early withdrawal calculator → How a 401(k) Loan Works and How Much You Can Borrow Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(A) , a new loan plus all your other outstanding loans from the plan must not exceed the lesser of two limits. The first limit is $50,000, reduced by the excess (if any) of your highest outstanding loan balance during the one-year period ending the day before the new loan is made over your outstanding balance on the day it is made. The second limit is the greater of one-half of your vested balance (your nonforfeitable accrued benefit under the plan) or $10,000. These three illustrations of the formula assume no prior loans. They are examples, not advice. A participant with a $15,000 vested balance: one-half of the balance is $7,500. Because the formula uses the greater of one-half of the vested balance or $10,000, the second limit is $10,000. Comparing $10,000 to the $50,000 maximum, the lesser figure is $10,000. The borrowing cap is $10,000. A participant with a $60,000 vested balance: one-half of the vested balance is $30,000. That figure is greater than $10,000. Comparing $30,000 to the $50,000 ceiling, the lesser figure is $30,000. The borrowing cap is $30,000. A participant with a $200,000 vested balance: one-half of the vested balance is $100,000. That figure exceeds $10,000, but federal law caps the maximum borrowing amount at the lesser of that figure or $50,000. The borrowing cap is $50,000. To run your own numbers, use the 401(k) loan calculator . Can a Solo 401(k) Lend to Its Owner? Yes, a solo 401(k) can lend to its owner when the plan document provides for loans, and the same 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2) limits apply. Lending between a plan and a disqualified person is generally a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(c)(1)(B) . The statute provides an exception for a loan to a disqualified person who is a plan participant or beneficiary, but a provision allowing loans is only one part of that exception. Under § 4975(d)(1), the loan must meet all five conditions: The loan must be available to all such participants or beneficiaries on a reasonably equivalent basis. Highly compensated employees must not be able to borrow larger amounts than other employees can borrow. The loan must follow specific provisions for loans set out in the plan. The loan must bear a reasonable rate of interest. The loan must be adequately secured. The loan exception is unavailable for lending to an owner of an individual retirement plan under § 4975(f)(6). A SEP, SIMPLE, or traditional individual retirement account (IRA) therefore cannot lend to its owner. That restriction does not categorically bar a solo 401(k) loan. Nothing in these conditions provides a workaround for borrowing from an IRA. For a different borrowing source, read 401(k) loan vs HELOC . An owner is generally a key employee because 26 U.S.C. § 416(i)(1)(A) includes a 5-percent owner in that category. Under § 72(p)(3), interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible during a period when the owner is a key employee. The plan document and its administrator determine whether a given loan meets the loan conditions. Run your balance through the 401(k) loan calculator . Repayment Rules and the Principal Residence Exception Federal law requires a 401(k) loan to be repaid within 5 years under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(i) . The terms of the loan agreement must require full repayment within that 5-year window from the date the loan is made. A loan term longer than 5 years fails the repayment rule unless the home purchase exception applies. The 5-year limit does not apply to a loan used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence ( 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(ii) ). That is determined when the loan is made. The longer term for such a loan is set by your plan, so ask your plan administrator. In addition to the term limit, 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(C) requires substantially level amortization of the loan over its entire term. Payments must be made not less frequently than quarterly. What Happens If a 401(k) Loan Is Not Repaid A plan loan is treated as having been received as a distribution under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(1)(A) if it does not meet the amount, 5-year term, and quarterly level-payment rules. A distribution can bring federal income tax. In addition to regular income tax, an early distribution can trigger an extra tax penalty. According to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Topic 558 , the law imposes a 10% additional tax on certain early distributions from retirement plans. Early distributions are generally distributions received before age 59½, though exceptions exist as detailed by the IRS. If a 401(k) loan balance is treated as a distribution to a borrower who has not reached age 59½, that borrower can face both income tax and the 10% additional tax on the unpaid amount. A separate rollover rule applies to a qualified plan loan offset amount. Under 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A) , the ordinary rollover window to deposit distributed funds into an eligible retirement plan or Individual Retirement Account (IRA) is 60 days after the distribution is received. However, for a qualified plan loan offset amount, 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(C)(i) provides an extended rollover deadline. You can complete a rollover of a qualified plan loan offset amount up to the due date, including tax extensions, for filing your federal income tax return for the tax year in which the amount is treated as distributed from the plan. Whether an offset qualifies requires specific analysis, so ask your plan administrator or a professional tax advisor about your situation. Plan-Specific Rules and Interest Deductibility Restrictions Federal statute authorizes employer plans to offer loans, but it does not require any plan to do so. Whether an employer retirement plan permits borrowing at all is decided entirely by the employer's plan document. If your plan does permit loans, the plan document also determines the application fees, ongoing administrative charges, the specific interest rate charged, the maximum number of loans you may have outstanding at one time, and the exact default procedures. Interest on a plan loan is not deductible in some cases, such as any period when you are a key employee or when the loan is secured by certain elective deferrals ( 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(3)(A) ). Ask your plan administrator or a tax professional whether either applies to you. Comparing a 401(k) Loan to Alternative Financing Options For another way to borrow, see our comparison of a 401(k) Loan vs HELOC . To explore debt payoff strategies, see our guide on How to Pay Off Debt . Next Steps for Requesting Your Plan Loan Documents Contact your employer's plan administrator to request a complete copy of the plan loan policy in writing. Review the document to confirm whether loans are permitted, the exact fees charged to originate and service the loan, the interest rate calculation method, and the plan's specific default timelines. Read your vested balance from your latest participant statement, then apply the lesser-of and greater-of formula from the first section. Frequently asked questions How much can I borrow from my 401(k)? Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(A), your loan plus all other outstanding plan loans must not exceed the lesser of $50,000 (reduced by any excess of your highest loan balance in the past year over your balance on the day the loan is made) or the greater of $10,000 or half your vested balance. With no prior loans, a $15,000 vested balance gives a $10,000 cap, $60,000 gives $30,000, and $200,000 gives $50,000. How long do I have to repay a 401(k) loan? Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(i), you must repay a 401(k) loan within 5 years from the date the loan is made. Repayment must occur through substantially level payments made at least quarterly over the term of the loan under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(C). The 5-year limit does not apply when loan proceeds are used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence. Do I pay taxes on a 401(k) loan? Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(1)(A), a loan from a qualified plan is treated as a distribution unless it meets the amount limit, the 5-year term, and the level quarterly payment rules. A distribution can bring regular income tax. If you are under age 59½, it can also bring the 10% additional tax described in IRS Topic 558, though exceptions exist. What happens to a 401(k) loan if I leave my job? What happens when you leave depends on your plan's default rules, so ask your plan administrator. If an unpaid balance is treated as a distribution, the ordinary rollover window is 60 days after the distribution is received (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A)). For a qualified plan loan offset amount, a rollover can be made up to the due date, including extensions, for filing the tax return for the year the amount is treated as distributed (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(C)(i)). Ask your plan administrator or a tax professional whether your offset qualifies. Can I borrow from my 401(k) to buy a house? Yes, if your employer plan allows it. Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(ii), the 5-year repayment limit does not apply to a loan used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence. The amount limit still applies, and repayment must still be made in substantially level payments at least quarterly. Can I take a loan from a solo 401(k)? Yes, you can take a loan from a solo 401(k) if its plan document provides for loans, and the same limits under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) apply. Avoiding a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1) takes more than a plan provision. The loan must also meet the other conditions in that section, and the plan document and its administrator decide whether a given loan does. An IRA-based plan, including a SEP, SIMPLE or traditional IRA, cannot lend to its owner under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(f)(6). For the full list of conditions, see the section "Can a Solo 401(k) Lend to Its Owner?" above. How does a solo 401(k) loan work? A solo 401(k) loan is possible if the plan document provides for loans. It must follow the same amount, term, and payment rules under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) and meet the other conditions in 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1). A loan provision in the plan document alone does not satisfy those conditions. An owner is generally a key employee under 26 U.S.C. § 416(i)(1)(A)(ii). Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(3), interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible. Use the 401(k) loan calculator to see the limit and payment for your balance. With no prior loans, a $15,000 vested balance gives a $10,000 cap, $60,000 gives $30,000, and $200,000 gives $50,000.

mainEntity.name: How long do I have to repay a 401(k) loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(i), you must repay a 401(k) loan within 5 years from the date the loan is made. Repayment must occur through substantially level payments made at least quarterly over the term of the loan under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(C). The 5-year limit does not apply when loan proceeds are used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence.

mainEntity.name: Do I pay taxes on a 401(k) loan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(1)(A), a loan from a qualified plan is treated as a distribution unless it meets the amount limit, the 5-year term, and the level quarterly payment rules. A distribution can bring regular income tax. If you are under age 59½, it can also bring the 10% additional tax described in IRS Topic 558, though exceptions exist.

mainEntity.name: What happens to a 401(k) loan if I leave my job?

acceptedAnswer.text: What happens when you leave depends on your plan's default rules, so ask your plan administrator. If an unpaid balance is treated as a distribution, the ordinary rollover window is 60 days after the distribution is received (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(A)). For a qualified plan loan offset amount, a rollover can be made up to the due date, including extensions, for filing the tax return for the year the amount is treated as distributed (26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(C)(i)). Ask your plan administrator or a tax professional whether your offset qualifies.

mainEntity.name: Can I borrow from my 401(k) to buy a house?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if your employer plan allows it. Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(2)(B)(ii), the 5-year repayment limit does not apply to a loan used to acquire a dwelling unit that is to be used within a reasonable time as your principal residence. The amount limit still applies, and repayment must still be made in substantially level payments at least quarterly.

mainEntity.name: Can I take a loan from a solo 401(k)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, you can take a loan from a solo 401(k) if its plan document provides for loans, and the same limits under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) apply. Avoiding a prohibited transaction under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1) takes more than a plan provision. The loan must also meet the other conditions in that section, and the plan document and its administrator decide whether a given loan does. An IRA-based plan, including a SEP, SIMPLE or traditional IRA, cannot lend to its owner under 26 U.S.C. § 4975(f)(6). For the full list of conditions, see the section "Can a Solo 401(k) Lend to Its Owner?" above.

mainEntity.name: How does a solo 401(k) loan work?

acceptedAnswer.text: A solo 401(k) loan is possible if the plan document provides for loans. It must follow the same amount, term, and payment rules under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p) and meet the other conditions in 26 U.S.C. § 4975(d)(1). A loan provision in the plan document alone does not satisfy those conditions. An owner is generally a key employee under 26 U.S.C. § 416(i)(1)(A)(ii). Under 26 U.S.C. § 72(p)(3), interest on the owner's own plan loan is not deductible. Use the 401(k) loan calculator to see the limit and payment for your balance.
